title: Passwords: stop remembering them
subtitle: Four rules, then five accounts to prove it

cards.title: Length is the only thing that buys time
cards.say: People hand me punctuation and think they've done something. A guesser's machine doesn't care about your exclamation mark. It cares how much there is to get through.

rules.headline: Long beats clever.
rules.body: Four or five unrelated words. A short password with symbols in it is still short.

rules.headline: Never the same one twice.
rules.body: One leaked site becomes five leaked sites by itself: attackers replay the pairs they already have.

cards.sign_off: Four unrelated words beat P@ssw0rd! by a distance no punctuation closes.

cards.title: The part nobody wants to hear
cards.say: You are not supposed to remember them. That is not a failure of yours, it is arithmetic. Nobody holds forty unrelated passwords in their head, so people reuse one, and that is the whole problem in one move.

rules.headline: Don't make it about you.
rules.body: Your name, your year of birth, your pet, your team. All of it is already online, and all of it is what anyone guessing tries first.

rules.headline: You are not supposed to remember them.
rules.body: That is the manager's job. You remember one strong passphrase and let it hold the rest.

cards.sign_off: One strong passphrase, a manager for the rest, and two-factor login where it is offered.

sections.intro: Right, this is the bit that actually fixes it. Pick one of these now, not later. They're all better than your memory, and four of the five cost nothing.

tools.name: Bitwarden
tools.what: Free, open-source, audited, syncs to every device.
tools.dog_says: My oldest pal. He remembers every password for you, and he won't fill one in on a fake site. If he stays quiet, that's your warning.

tools.name: Proton Pass
tools.what: Swiss, free tier, same account as Proton Mail.
tools.dog_says: Younger than the others, and run here in Switzerland. Good pick if you already use their mail.

tools.name: KeePassXC
tools.what: Keeps everything in a file on your own device. No company involved.
tools.dog_says: For the sort who trusts nobody. Fair enough, friend. Just remember the backups are yours too.

tools.name: 1Password
tools.what: Paid, and the easiest to set up for a whole family.
tools.dog_says: Costs money, I'll say it plainly. Worth it if you're sorting this out for your parents as well.

tools.name: The one already on your phone
tools.what: Apple Passwords, Google Password Manager or Firefox.
tools.dog_says: Already there, already backed up, nothing to install. Tied to one ecosystem, so it's awkward if you switch. Still far better than reusing one.

sections.question: How are you feeling about this?

levels.label: Still unsure
levels.reply: That's quite all right, dear. You only need to do one thing today: install one of Dog's managers. The rest follows from that, and we'll go slowly.

levels.label: Getting there
levels.reply: Good. Now prove it on five accounts in a row, because that is where remembering stops working.

levels.label: Confident
levels.reply: Confident, are we? Then five accounts should be no trouble at all. I'll be waiting at the end to show you which one I'd have cracked first.

cards.title: Now the part that proves it
cards.say: Knowing the rules is free. Five accounts in a row is where it costs something, because by the third one your memory gives up and the manager is the only way through. That is the lesson, and you cannot read it, you have to feel it.

rules.headline: Five sites, five new passwords.
rules.body: All pretend, all ours, and they unlock nothing. Do not use a password you really have, not even once.

rules.headline: Save each one as you go.
rules.body: In the manager you just installed. Not in a note, not in your head.

rules.headline: We will ask for one of them back.
rules.body: In a later session, one of the five picked at random. We will not say which, so the only way through is to have saved all five. We cannot remind you: we never kept them.

cards.sign_off: Five accounts. Then we find out whether the habit is real.
